The mantle cloak concept was introduced in 2009 by Andrea Alù as a surface cloaking technique.
Mantle cloaks use patterned metasurfaces with negligible thickness to achieve cloaking.
Traditional metamaterial cloaks require volumetric layers with finite thickness.
The mantle cloak operates by tailoring the surface impedance to cancel scattering harmonics.
Numerical simulations show up to 97% scattering reduction for a dielectric sphere with permittivity 10 and diameter λ0/5.
For a conducting sphere of the same size, the mantle cloak achieves about 86% scattering reduction.
The surface reactance for optimal cloaking in the dielectric example is approximately 175 Ω.
The mantle cloak can be conformal to the object surface, requiring no or minimal spacing for dielectric objects.
A small spacing is necessary between the mantle cloak and conducting objects to avoid shorting effects.
The mantle cloak exhibits relatively broad bandwidth performance compared to volumetric metamaterial cloaks.
The cloak’s performance is quasi-isotropic and largely independent of wave polarization and incidence angle.
The mantle cloak allows electromagnetic fields to penetrate inside the cloaked region, enabling sensing applications.
Theoretical analysis uses Mie scattering theory and boundary conditions involving surface impedance.
Full-wave simulations validate the mantle cloak design and show field distributions consistent with scattering reduction.
The mantle cloak induces enhanced magnetic fields near the surface and electric fields inside the object.
Frequency selective surfaces (FSS) are key enabling structures for realizing the mantle cloak.
The mantle cloak concept can be extended to terahertz and optical frequencies using plasmonic metasurfaces.
Cascaded reactive surfaces may enable multifrequency operation or suppression of multiple scattering orders.
The mantle cloak is inherently low-profile, conformal, and simpler to fabricate than volumetric metamaterial cloaks.
The mantle cloak approach is based on destructive interference and scattering cancellation mechanisms.
